title: What Can You Actually Gain From Having a Mentor?
excerpt: A good mentor can help you see opportunities you might have missed, navigate difficult situations and develop the confidence to take your next step. But the real value of mentoring goes beyond advice, it's about building the skills, judgement and independence to shape your own future.
content:
At some point in your career, you might wonder whether having a mentor would make any difference. Perhaps you're facing a challenge at work, weighing up your next career move or thinking about stepping into a leadership role. You might have a good idea of what you want to achieve without being sure how to get there.

A good mentor can't guarantee success or make difficult decisions for you. What they can offer is a different perspective, the benefit of their experience, and support in recognising what you're capable of.

I particularly like this quote:

> "A mentor is someone who sees more ability and talent within you than you see yourself. And they don't just stop there; they bring the attributes out of you!"

I think it captures what mentoring is for. Passing on knowledge and advice is part of it, but the bigger part is helping someone recognise their potential and giving them the confidence and tools to make the most of it.

## A different perspective

When you're dealing with a difficult situation, it's easy to get caught up in the details and lose sight of the bigger picture. A mentor can help you step back, challenge your assumptions and consider options you might have missed.

Whether it's a difficult conversation, a problem at work or a decision about what to do next in your career, talking it through with someone who has faced similar situations can help you see it differently. They won't always have the right answer, but sometimes the right question is enough to help you find your own.

## Learning from experience

You can learn a lot by working things out for yourself, but some lessons take a long time, and others are uncomfortable. A mentor can share the experiences, mistakes and lessons that have shaped their own career, so you have a better idea of what to look out for and what you might do differently.

This is especially useful when you're facing something new, such as your first leadership role or a step up in responsibility. You still need to build your own experience, but you don't have to start entirely from scratch.

## Building confidence and recognising your potential

It's surprisingly easy to underestimate yourself, especially when you're surrounded by more experienced people or taking on responsibilities you've never had before. You might question whether you're ready for the next opportunity, or focus so much on what you don't know that you overlook what you already offer.

A good mentor can help you recognise your strengths, spot areas to develop and challenge the assumptions that might be holding you back. Sometimes you need encouragement. At other times you need someone to be honest about where you could improve.

Confidence should grow from what you learn and achieve, though, more than from someone telling you you're good enough. A mentor can help you see your potential, but turning it into action is up to you.

## Becoming more independent

For me, this is one of the most important outcomes of mentoring. You shouldn't end up needing to ask your mentor what to do every time you face a challenge. The aim is to develop the judgement and confidence to make those decisions yourself.

Over time, you should get better at recognising problems, weighing up options and deciding how to move forward. You might still want to talk your thinking through with your mentor, but you'll be doing it for another perspective, with the decision staying yours. Their experience is there to help you build your own.

## Is having a mentor worth it?

I believe mentoring can be extremely worthwhile, as long as you're willing to take responsibility for your own development. A mentor can offer guidance, perspective, honest feedback and encouragement, but they can't do the work for you. You still have to make the decisions, learn from your mistakes and put what you've learned into practice.

You don't need to have everything figured out before looking for a mentor, either. You might have a clear career goal, or you might just know you want to grow without being sure where to start. Both are good reasons to have a conversation.

In the end, what matters most is what changes after each conversation: the decisions you feel more confident making, the challenges you're better equipped to handle and the opportunities you're willing to go after. A good mentor can help you see what you could become, and a good mentoring relationship helps you build the confidence, skills and judgement to get there yourself.
